tasks.description: Create a custom exception class `InvalidAgeError` that inherits from Exception. Raise it when age < 0. Test with age = -5.
tasks.hint:
`class InvalidAgeError(Exception): pass` — just inherit from Exception.
Raise it: `if age < 0: raise InvalidAgeError(f'Age cannot be negative: {age}')`
Catch it: `except InvalidAgeError as e: print(e)`
tasks.walkthrough:
The class body is just `pass`; inheriting from Exception is all it takes.
`raise` with a message stops the function, and the `except` block catches it by its new name.

tasks.description: Catch multiple exception types in separate except blocks: handle ZeroDivisionError and ValueError differently.
tasks.hint:
You can have multiple `except` clauses — Python uses the FIRST matching one.
`try: # code that might raise
except ZeroDivisionError: print('No division by zero!')
except ValueError: print('Invalid value!')`
Or catch both at once: `except (ZeroDivisionError, ValueError):`
tasks.walkthrough:
'2' works. '0' converts fine but the division fails, hitting the first handler.
'abc' fails at `int()`, which raises ValueError and hits the second handler.

tasks.description: Use `raise from` to re-raise an exception with more context. Catch a KeyError and raise a custom error that includes the original.
tasks.hint:
`raise CustomError('message') from original_exception` chains the exceptions.
The original exception is attached and shown in the traceback for debugging.
`except KeyError as e: raise ValueError(f'Key not found: {e}') from e`
tasks.walkthrough:
The inner `except` catches the KeyError and raises a ValueError with a clearer message.
`from e` links the two, so the original KeyError is available as `__cause__` and appears in a full traceback.

tasks.description: Write a function that validates a username: must be 3-20 chars, alphanumeric only. Raise ValueError with a descriptive message if invalid.
tasks.hint:
Check length: `if not (3 <= len(name) <= 20): raise ValueError('Username must be 3-20 characters')`
Check characters: `if not name.isalnum(): raise ValueError('Only letters and numbers allowed')`
Test with valid AND invalid inputs.
tasks.walkthrough:
Each rule gets its own check and its own message, so the caller knows exactly what was wrong.
The loop tests one valid name and three invalid ones to exercise every branch.

tasks.description: Use `warnings.warn()` to issue a deprecation warning for an old function, then call the new one.
tasks.hint:
`import warnings`
Inside the old function: `warnings.warn('Use new_func() instead', DeprecationWarning, stacklevel=2)`
This warns the developer without crashing the program.
tasks.walkthrough:
`warnings.warn` sends the message to stderr and returns; the program keeps running.
`stacklevel=2` makes the warning point at the caller of `old_greet`, which is where the fix needs to happen.
`simplefilter('always')` makes sure the warning is shown, since DeprecationWarnings are hidden by default in some contexts.

lesson.intro:
You can catch errors. Today you'll also make your own: raising exceptions on
purpose when input is bad, defining custom error types so callers can tell
problems apart, and chaining errors so the original cause isn't lost.

sections.heading: Custom exceptions
sections.body:
An exception is just a class that inherits from `Exception`. Usually the
body is `pass`; the name is what matters. Raise it with `raise` and a
message, catch it by name.

sections.heading: Several except blocks
sections.body:
Different errors can get different handling. Python picks the first
`except` that matches. A tuple catches several with the same handler.
sections.output:
No division by zero!
Invalid value!

sections.heading: raise ... from: keep the cause
sections.body:
When you catch a low-level error and raise a clearer one, `from e` attaches
the original so it still shows in the traceback. The new error's
`__cause__` is the old one.

sections.heading: Validation that fails loudly
sections.body:
A function that checks its input and raises `ValueError` with a specific
message is far easier to use than one that quietly returns the wrong thing.
sections.output:
bad: Only letters and numbers allowed
bad: Username must be 3-20 characters
ok: sam1

sections.heading: Warnings
sections.body:
Sometimes you want to flag something without stopping. `warnings.warn`
prints a message to stderr and carries on. In this app, warnings show up
in the output panel under a separate heading.

watch_out: Raising a string, `raise 'oops'`, isn't allowed. Raise an exception object.
Catching `Exception` in a bare way hides bugs. Catch what you expect.
`raise` on its own inside an `except` re-raises the same error, which is handy when you only wanted to log it.
A custom exception with no message prints as an empty string. Always pass one.
